images.caption: Figure 2:Overview of DexDuet.(a) A human demonstration provides the object trajectory, which gives the policyπθ\pi_{\theta}the next object pose, and the hand motion, which is retargeted to a reference motion that the robot hands imitate. Insideπθ\pi_{\theta}, two per-hand policies share one network, and each maps its own observation𝐨\mathbf{o}and the partner observation𝐳\mathbf{z}to an action𝐚\mathbf{a}. (b) Two interaction rewards compare each robot hand with the human hand relative to the object. The hand graph reward compares the palm and finger directions and the fingertip gaps, and the hand-object contact reward compares the distance and the closest point of each hand region to the object. (c) A-RSI gives each segmentbbof the demonstration its own assistance levelhbh_{b}, which it lowers (green) or raises (red), never above a ceilingh¯​(u)\bar{h}(u)that decreases over the updatesuu. Episodes start from states that the policy has reached, and their start segment is drawn fromp⁡(b)p(b), which favors the segments with a high failure ratefbf_{b}.

Figure 3:Qualitative comparison with the baselines.The robot is named above each column. The first four columns are Box-200, Ketchup-100, Mixer-170 and Notebook-300 from the DexMachina suite. Each pairs a DexMachina[30]checkpoint with a DexDuet run whose ADD-AUC differs by at most 3 points. The last two columns are the spray bottle and basket episodes of V2D, where the baseline is CHORD[63]. Soft patches mark where the left (teal) and right (violet) hand touch the object.

Figure 4:Real-world demonstrations.DexDuet’s simulated rollouts replayed on real robots. (a) A Unitree G1 with Inspire hands places a box on the floor. (b) Two Franka arms with Allegro hands reorient a bottle and (c) place a gamepad on a block.

Figure S1:Interaction rewards and Contact-AUC on hands with fewer fingers.Each robot finger is matched to the human finger it is retargeted from, and the human fingers without a robot counterpart (grey) are left out of both rewards.
(a) The hand graph keeps the edges𝐞j\mathbf{e}_{j}and the fingertip gaps (dashed) of the matched fingers.
On the human and the robot hand, the palm normal𝐧\mathbf{n}is spanned by the index base and the outermost finger base that the robot hand has (orange lines).
Dex3 has no finger base beyond the middle finger, so its normal is a fixed axis of the palm link, calibrated once per episode to the human normal, which keeps the little base.
For Dex3, the human and robot palm directions𝐞0\mathbf{e}_{0}point to the midpoint of the index and middle bases.
(b) The hand-object contact reward compares the palm and the outer segments of the matched fingers.
(c) Contact-AUC needs no finger matching.
Its contact points𝒞^w\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{w}are all points of the robot hand near the part, from any finger, which are the keypoints within 1.5 cm on the DexMachina suite and the surface points within 5 mm on V2D.
Their driftδ^w\hat{\delta}_{w}is scored on the windows in which the human hand holds the part with a driftδ~w\tilde{\delta}_{w}below 1 cm.
A tilde marks the human hand and a hat the robot hand.

Figure S2:How RSI, a VOC curriculum and A-RSI handle a hard segment(illustration).
Each line is an episode, drawn from the state it starts from (card).
RSI[35]starts from reference states.
The hands of these states do not hold the object, so the episodes end at once, and only the episodes that start at the first frame learn.
A VOC curriculum[30,63]holds the object with one level and lowers it only when episodes reach the end.
Once episodes are stopped at the hard segment, the level stalls, and so does training (Fig.S3).
A-RSI gives each segment its own level under a deadline ceilingh¯​(u)\bar{h}(u).
It starts episodes from keyframes, which are states reached in earlier episodes, and starts most of them where the policy fails, with probabilityp⁡(b)p(b)computed from the failure ratesfbf_{b}(Eq.11).

Figure S4:Runs that track the object equally well can differ in contact preservation.(a) Mixer-170 and (b) Notebook-300 with Inspire hands, each a released DexMachina[30]checkpoint and a DexDuet run with almost the same ADD-AUC. In the marked frames, both objects are within 2 cm of the demonstration and DexDuet preserves the human’s contact, whereas DexMachina’s fingers slide on the part that the human holds or its hand leaves that part (dashed circles).

Figure S5:DexDuet on the DexMachina suite.Columns, from left, are Box-200, Ketchup-100, Ketchup-300, Mixer-170, Mixer-300, Notebook-300 and Waffleiron-300, and rows show the human demonstration and DexDuet with Inspire, Allegro, XHand and Schunk hands. Each robot row is the seed with the median Contact-AUC, each column is shown at the human hold with both hands closest to the middle of the demonstration from one camera, and soft patches mark where the left (teal) and right (violet) hand touch the object.

Figure S6:CHORD and DexDuet on V2Dwith the Unitree G1 and its Dex3 hands. Columns, from left, are episodes 3 (mug), 5 (box), 14 (round table), 16 (spray bottle), 27 (basket) and 28 (squeegee), and rows show the human with SOMA hands, CHORD[63]trained with PPO and DexDuet, each in its first scored rollout at the same training budget. Each column is shown at the human hold closest to the middle of the episode from one camera, and at that moment CHORD has lost the object in every column except the box.

Figure S7:Real-world replays on the Unitree G1with Inspire hands. (a) The robot lowers a box from chest height, places it on the floor and stands up. (b) It carries a bag and puts it down on the floor. (c) It pushes an office chair while walking.
Figure S8:Real-world replays on two Franka armswith Allegro hands. (a) Both hands reorient a bottle that they hold above the table. (b) Both hands place a gamepad on a block.
